summary: Three kinds of robot pet share one battery-checking rule that lives in the base class, and each subclass calls that rule with super() before describing its own talent. The battery value itself is guarded by a property setter that clamps it to the range 0-100.

lines.text: The base class holds everything the three pets have in common: a name, a validated battery level, a mood, and the shared rule about performing on low power.

lines.code: self.battery = battery  # uses the property setter for validation
lines.text: Assigning to self.battery here does not create a plain attribute; because battery is a property, this call runs the setter and the value is checked before it is stored.
The @property decorator turns the method below it into a read-only-looking attribute, so callers write pet.battery rather than pet.battery().
The real value lives in _battery, and the leading underscore signals that outside code should go through the property instead.
This registers the following method as the code that runs whenever anything assigns to battery, which is where validation belongs.
A negative battery makes no sense, so the setter quietly corrects it rather than trusting the caller.
Anything above full charge is clamped down to 100, keeping the stored value inside a meaningful range.
The base version does not describe a trick at all; it only handles the two battery problems that every pet shares.
With a dead battery there is no performance of any kind, so this case is caught first.
Returning None is the signal that the battery is fine and the subclass should go ahead with its own talent.
RobotCat inherits the initializer and the battery property, so it only needs to add what makes a cat different.
super() reaches the base class version, letting the cat reuse the shared battery check instead of copying that logic into every subclass.
A non-empty string means the base class already had something to say, so the cat returns that message and skips its trick.

lines.code: return f"{self.name} gracefully balances on two legs! (Battery: {self.battery}%)"
lines.text: This is the part unique to a cat, reached only once the shared check has passed.
Creating a subclass instance runs the base class __init__, since RobotCat never defines its own.
Putting different types in one list works because they all answer to show_talent().
The same call produces a different talent for each pet: Python looks up show_talent on the object's actual class, which is polymorphism at work.
